section_summary: This section comprises monthly political reports, despatches, and memoranda from the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo and the State Department spanning December 1931 through May 1932. It details major military and diplomatic developments in the Far East, including the Japanese occupation of Chinchow and Harbin, the outbreak and armistice of the Shanghai Incident, and the creation of Manchukuo under Henry Pu-Yi. Domestically, it documents severe political upheaval in Japan, including the collapse of the Wakatsuki Cabinet, the installation of the Inukai Cabinet, the reimposition of the gold embargo, and a wave of ultra-nationalist violence culminating in the assassinations of Junnosuke Inouye and Baron Takuma Dan by the Blood Brotherhood.

subfiles.about: Continuation of the Tokyo Embassy's monthly political report on conditions in Japan for December 1931.
subfiles.from: Embassy of the United States of America, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: The concluding portion of the December 1931 report addresses foreign relations, including an alleged Czech plot in Moscow and the Geneva Disarmament Conference. It describes the domestic political crisis precipitated by remarks regarding Chinchow, resulting in the fall of the Wakatsuki Cabinet and the formation of the Seiyukai Cabinet under Prime Minister Inukai. Furthermore, it details the reimposition of the gold embargo, suspension of note conversion, financial fallout involving the Mitsui interests and Yokohama Specie Bank, and provides complete lists of despatches and telegrams sent to Washington during December 1931.
subfiles.title: Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of December, 1931 (Report No. 63)

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch transmitting Report No. 64 on political, military, and economic conditions in Japan for January 1932.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 488 transmits the Embassy's comprehensive review of January 1932. It documents U.S.-Japanese diplomatic correspondence concerning the non-recognition note and the assault on Consul Chamberlain in Mukden. It covers the occupation of Chinchow, military operations against General Ting Chao at Harbin, the initial armed clashes in Shanghai, the Korean assassination attempt against Emperor Hirohito (Sakuradamon Incident) leading to the Cabinet's resignation offer, the dissolution of the Imperial Diet, and lists of diplomatic communications sent in January.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 488: Report on Conditions in Japan for the Month of January, 1932 (Report No. 64)

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch transmitting Report No. 65 on Japanese political, economic, and foreign affairs during February 1932.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 517 transmits the monthly report for February 1932, detailing Japanese press reaction to Secretary Stimson's letter to Senator Borah and apprehensions over an American boycott. It traces the full-scale escalation of hostilities in Shanghai by the Japanese Army and Navy against the 19th Route Army, the capture of Harbin, and the formal declaration of Manchurian autonomy. On the home front, it records Prince Fushimi's appointment as Navy Chief of Staff, the assassination of former Finance Minister Junnosuke Inouye, the overwhelming general election victory of the Seiyukai Party, and logs of February despatches and telegrams.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 517: Political Report for February, 1932 (Report No. 65)

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing significant developments reported in the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report for March 1932.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: This Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum extracts crucial points from the Tokyo Embassy's March political report. It highlights the inauguration ceremony and impending recognition of Manchukuo, along with official casualty figures for the Manchurian and Shanghai campaigns totaling 768 killed and 2,976 wounded. Additionally, it notes increasing Japanese press advocacy for withdrawal from the League of Nations, internal Cabinet dissension within the Seiyukai, and an unfavorable trade balance.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Monthly Political Report for March, 1932 (Summary Memorandum)

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch transmitting Report No. 66 on political, economic, and military conditions in Japan during March 1932.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Charge d'Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 560 transmits Report No. 66 covering March 1932. It records Henry Pu-Yi's installation as Chief Executive of Manchukuo, the military reduction of the Woosung forts leading to a ceasefire and difficult peace talks in Shanghai, and mutual Russo-Japanese border assurances under the Portsmouth Treaty. Domestically, it chronicles the Sixty-First Diet session approving emergency war appropriations, Cabinet friction culminating in Suzuki replacing Nakahashi, the assassination of Baron Takuma Dan revealing the terroristic 'Blood Brotherhood' conspiracy, the departure of Ambassador Forbes, and attached schedules of despatches and telegrams.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 560: Embassy's Report on Conditions in the Month of March, 1932 (Report No. 66)

subfiles.about: Internal State Department routing slip recording the transfer of file 894.00PR.
subfiles.summary: This internal administrative filing and routing slip records the handling of file 894.00PR within the Department of State. Dated April 8, 1932, it bears the initials of clerk CFH and notes routing to FE-Amrine in the Division of Far Eastern Affairs.
subfiles.title: Filing and Routing Slip for File 894.00PR

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch transmitting Report No. 68 on conditions in Japan for May 1932.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Charge d'Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 634 submits Report No. 68 covering events in May 1932. It reviews relations with the United States, including a bombing at the Nagasaki Consulate, threats against foreign legations, and Foreign Minister Yoshizawa's proposal for an informal Tokyo conference on Shanghai. It details the signing of the Shanghai armistice agreement on May 5, subsequent troop withdrawals, deaths of bomb victims General Shirakawa and Mr. Kawabata, widespread guerrilla fighting against Manchukuo authorities, the investigations of the League of Nations Commission under Lord Lytton, the collapse of the Seiyukai Cabinet after the May 15 incident, and the formation of a national unity Cabinet under Admiral Saito.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 634: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan for the Month of May, 1932 (Report No. 68)
